query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under oxidizing conditions at elevated temperatures, degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is governed by selective oxidation of its most reactive elements (Al and Ti). This leads to the formation of a continuous brittle oxide scale (predominantly Al2O3 and/or TiOx) at grain boundaries and on the surface, which, due to thermal expansion mismatch, eventually spalls or cracks, triggering localized embrittlement and catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix.
generation.intervention: Reduce the oxygen partial pressure in the gas environment during the elevated-temperature exposure relative to the baseline oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Exposures are conducted at the specified elevated temperature with all variables controlled except for the oxygen partial pressure. One set of samples is exposed to the baseline (standard) oxidizing gas composition and another set to a gas composition with reduced oxygen content, while other parameters (temperature, exposure duration, gas flow rate) remain constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous brittle oxide scale (primarily consisting of Al2O3/TiOx) that forms along the grain boundaries and surfaces of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of aluminum and titanium causes a rapid formation of a brittle oxide layer. Under elevated temperatures, the mismatch in thermal expansion between the oxide scale and the underlying fcc matrix induces high localized stresses. This ultimately leads to scale spallation and crack formation, which in turn act as stress concentrators that promote catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: By lowering the oxygen partial pressure, the rate and continuity of the oxide scale formation will be reduced relative to the baseline condition. This should delay oxide-induced cracking and extend the time to catastrophic failure, as observed by a lower crack density and improved mechanical integrity in the reduced oxygen condition.
generation.baseline: Exposure of the alloy under a standard oxidizing atmosphere at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within the operational range of elevated temperatures and controlled oxidizing/reducing environments specified. Effects outside this temperature and gas composition window remain untested.
generation.uncertainty: While selective oxidation is a known degradation mechanism in similar alloys, the quantitative influence of oxygen partial pressure on the scale formation kinetics and subsequent mechanical failure timing in this specific HEA remains somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples. Subject one set to elevated-temperature exposure in a baseline oxidizing atmosphere and the other set in a reduced oxygen partial pressure atmosphere. Continuously monitor oxide scale formation via surface and cross-sectional electron microscopy, record crack initiation events and density, and perform mechanical testing to assess time-to-failure and overall mechanical integrity.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (using scanning electron microscopy)
Crack density and initiation (using optical or electron microscopy)
Mechanical integrity/time-to-failure (via tensile or fatigue testing)
Chemical composition of the oxide scale (using energy dispersive spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples exposed to reduced oxygen partial pressure do not exhibit a significant delay or reduction in continuous oxide scale formation, do not show a measurable decrease in crack density, or do not demonstrate improved time-to-failure compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation governs degradation via brittle scale formation is falsified.
